description.summary: An unidentified creature reported in and around Enfield, Illinois during a brief sighting cluster in late April and early May 1973, described as a roughly four-and-a-half-foot-tall, gray, three-legged entity with two short arms and pink eyes.
description.full: The Enfield Horror (also Enfield Monster) is an unidentified creature reported in Enfield, Illinois, in April and May 1973. The principal witness, Henry McDaniel, reported being scratched at and confronted by an entity at his home about 10 PM on April 25, 1973: he described a creature about four and a half feet tall, gray-coloured, with three legs, a short body, two short arms, and pink eyes 'as big as flashlights'. McDaniel fired four shots at the creature with a pistol; it hissed (compared to a wildcat) and fled across the yard in long bounding leaps. A reported earlier encounter the same night by 10-year-old Greg Garrett was later admitted by the boy to Western Illinois University researchers to have been a hoax. McDaniel reported a second encounter near the railroad on May 6, 1973, and a search party led by WWKI radio's Rick Rainbow reported seeing and recording a similar 'apelike' creature in an abandoned building. Police investigators noted dog-like footprints with six toe pads in the soft earth and described McDaniel as rational and sober. White County Sheriff Roy Poshard Jr. publicly threatened to arrest McDaniel for continuing to discuss the creature. Five out-of-town men who arrived armed to hunt the creature were charged with hunting violations. Western Illinois University researchers later concluded that only three first-hand reports existed, amplified by media into an apparent 'epidemic'. Proposed mundane explanations include an escaped kangaroo (rejected by McDaniel), a wild ape, large dogs, bears, deer, and wildcats.

etymology.origin: Named after Enfield, a small village in White County, Illinois, USA, where the 1973 sightings occurred.
etymology.meaning: 'Enfield Horror' / 'Enfield Monster' is descriptive English coined by local and national press during the 1973 reports.
etymology.first_use: Local Illinois press coverage of April–May 1973.

related_phenomena.name: Flatwoods Monster
related_phenomena.description: 1952 West Virginia 'high-strangeness' humanoid cryptid often grouped with Enfield by researchers.

related_phenomena.name: Hopkinsville Goblins
related_phenomena.description: 1955 Kentucky home-invasion entity case often grouped with Enfield.

features.description: Witness Henry McDaniel reported the creature had three legs.
Two small, short arms set on a short body.
Large, prominent pink eyes were a distinctive part of the witness description.
Made a hiss compared by McDaniel to a wildcat's call.

physical.morphology: Reported as a small, gray humanoid with a short body, two short arms, three legs, and large pink eyes; locomotion involved long bounding leaps.

abilities.description: McDaniel reported the creature covered approximately fifty feet in three jumps as it fled toward a railway embankment.
McDaniel fired four shots; the creature appeared unharmed and fled.

patterns: Reported only at night during the April–May 1973 cluster
Active in residential and rail-adjacent locations near Enfield

range.description: Reports limited to a small area in and around Enfield, Illinois, during a six-week window in 1973; no documented reports outside this geographic and temporal cluster.

hotspots.name: Henry McDaniel residence, Enfield

location.description: Henry McDaniel's home and adjacent yard in the village of Enfield, Illinois

hotspots.notes: Site of McDaniel's two reported encounters (25 April 1973 and 6 May 1973).

first_recorded.source: Henry McDaniel's encounter, reported to White County police and local Illinois press

peak_activity_periods.description: Entire reported sighting cluster of the Enfield Horror

origins.cultural_roots: Single Midwestern American sighting cluster, occurring during a peak period of high-strangeness cryptid reports in the United States.
origins.earliest_accounts: Henry McDaniel's police report and local Illinois press coverage from April 25, 1973 onward.
origins.folklore_connections: Often grouped with the Flatwoods Monster (1952), Hopkinsville Goblins (1955), and Mothman (1966–67) as 'high-strangeness' humanoid cryptid cases of the mid-20th-century United States.

timeline.event: Henry McDaniel reports an encounter with the creature at his home in Enfield, Illinois, around 10 PM, firing four shots at it
timeline.source: White County police records / Wikipedia: Enfield Monster

timeline.event: Earlier the same evening (~9:30 PM), 10-year-old Greg Garrett reports an encounter; later admits to Western Illinois University researchers it was a hoax

McDaniel reports a second encounter near a railroad trestle around 3 AM; a search party led by WWKI news director Rick Rainbow reports seeing and recording an apelike creature in an abandoned building
Five young out-of-town men arrive in Enfield armed with rifles and shotguns; the White County sheriff describes them as 'out drinking and raising hell' and they are charged with hunting violations
timeline.significance: Demonstrates the public-order impact of the reports

timeline.event: Western Illinois University researchers publish an analysis concluding that only three firsthand reports exist, amplified into an apparent 'epidemic' by media coverage
timeline.significance: Standard sociological reading of the case

history.modern_era: The Enfield Horror is a recurring entry in cryptid encyclopedias, podcasts (e.g. Astonishing Legends episode 232, 2022), and regional Illinois lore. There have been no significant new reports since the original 1973 cluster.

notable.name: Henry McDaniel first encounter

credibility_factors: Police described him as rational and sober
Reported physical scratching at his door

notable.description: About 10 PM, McDaniel heard scratching at his front door, took a flashlight and pistol outside, and saw a creature between two rosebushes: about four and a half feet tall, gray, with three legs, two short arms, and pink eyes. The creature hissed at him; he fired four shots at it; it bounded away in long leaps and was lost from sight near the railroad.
evidence: Dog-like footprints with six toe pads found in nearby soft earth

factors: Sheriff publicly hostile to ongoing claims
credibility.notes: The founding incident of the Enfield Horror case.

notable.name: Greg Garrett encounter (later admitted hoax)
notable.description: Greg Garrett, a 10-year-old neighbour of McDaniel, reported earlier the same evening that the creature stepped on his feet and tore his tennis shoes to shreds. He later told Western Illinois University researchers that the report was a hoax meant 'to tease Mr. M and have fun with an out of town newsman'.

credibility.notes: Important counter-data point in the case.

notable.name: McDaniel second encounter and WWKI search-party report

location.description: Railroad trestles near Enfield, Illinois, and a nearby abandoned building

types: Rick Rainbow (WWKI news director) and party
credibility_factors: Multiple witnesses in the search-party episode

notable.description: Around 3 AM McDaniel called WWKI radio reporting another sighting near railroad trestles. A search party led by WWKI news director Rick Rainbow later reported observing and recording an 'apelike' creature in an abandoned building.
evidence: Reported audio recording (subsequently not independently verified)

credibility.notes: Final substantive incident in the case.

physical.name: Dog-like footprints with six toe pads
physical.description: Police investigators found dog-like footprints with six toe pads in soft earth near McDaniel's home.
physical.analysis: No casts or photographs are widely cited in the secondary literature; the prints are described in police summaries.

audio.name: WWKI search-party recording
audio.description: Audio recording reportedly made by a search party led by WWKI news director Rick Rainbow at an abandoned building near the railroad.
audio.analysis: Cited in contemporary news coverage; not independently authenticated in the available secondary literature.

documentary.name: Western Illinois University analysis
documentary.description: Sociological analysis from Western Illinois University concluding that only three firsthand reports exist and that the case was amplified by media coverage and local gossip.
documentary.analysis: Standard skeptical / sociological reading of the Enfield Horror case.
documentary.source: Western Illinois University (1978) / Wikipedia: Enfield Monster

paranormal.name: High-strangeness cryptid
paranormal.description: Treats the Enfield Horror as a real but anomalous biological or paranormal entity, grouped with the Flatwoods Monster, Hopkinsville Goblins, and other 1950s–70s 'high-strangeness' humanoid cryptids.
proponents: Astonishing Legends and similar paranormal podcasts

scientific.name: Escaped kangaroo or wallaby
scientific.description: Some contemporary reporters proposed an escaped kangaroo from a private collection or zoo, given reports of bounding locomotion.

scientific.name: Wild ape or large primate
scientific.description: An anthropology student suggested an ape, citing parallel reports of similar creatures in Mississippi since 1941.
evidence_cited: Reported 'apelike' figure in WWKI search-party episode

skeptical.name: Misidentification + media amplification
skeptical.description: A small number of misidentifications of large dogs, bears, deer, or wildcats was amplified by sensational media coverage and local gossip into an apparent 'epidemic' of monster reports.
evidence_cited: WIU finding of only three firsthand reports

skeptical.name: Collective behavior / mass-panic episode
skeptical.description: The case is cited by sociologists as an example of collective behavior in which an isolated incident generates wider 'panic, hysteria, collective vision, and extreme suggestibility' under media pressure.

stories: Henry McDaniel's account of firing four shots at a three-legged creature in his yard
Greg Garrett's later-retracted account of having his shoes torn by the creature
The WWKI search-party 'apelike' encounter at the abandoned building
folklore.beliefs: The case is preserved largely in local Illinois lore and cryptid-enthusiast media.

literature: Coverage in cryptozoology encyclopedias and regional Illinois lore books
other: Astonishing Legends podcast, Episode 232: 'The Enfield Horror and Other Midwest Monsters' (2022)

researchers.name: Rick Rainbow
researchers.contribution: Led the May 6, 1973 search-party episode and reported audio recording

researchers.name: Western Illinois University researchers
researchers.contribution: 1978 sociological analysis treating the case as a media-amplified collective-behavior episode

researchers.name: Loren Coleman
researchers.contribution: Documentation of the Enfield Horror within standard cryptozoological reference works

organizations.name: International Cryptozoology Museum
organizations.focus: Cryptozoological curation including 1970s American humanoid cryptid cases

research.ongoing_studies: No active scientific or cryptozoological field investigation of the Enfield Horror is currently documented; the case is treated historically rather than as an ongoing phenomenon.
